fig:ex_schematic: Information-to-action feedback in the worked example.
fig:impulse_w0_first: Impulse responses to the first state shock dW⁰₀ with p₁=3, p₂=10, and r₁=r₂=0.1.
fig:mean_response_precision: Equilibrium mean control D̄¹ₜ as signal precision p varies (spectral solution, both players at precision p).
fig:costs_private_vs_pooled: Equilibrium costs under private signals (dashed) and a pooled signal (solid), with p₁=3 fixed and p₂ varying from 0.1 to 1000 on a logarithmic axis (spectral solution).
fig:precision_decomposition: Equilibrium quantities across the precision split, p₁+p₂=P̄=20, with opposing targets, σ=0.5, and asymmetric effort costs (r₁,r₂)=(0.05,0.2).
fig:delayed_birth_geometry: Observation and filter geometry under delay.
fig:stationary-filter: Decomposition by primitive shock of the W⁰ channel of the stationary filter kernel f¹(b*,a) at two coordinate ages b*.
fig:stationary-adjoint: The stationary two-sided state price h^(X,1)(ℓ) in the symmetric two-player benchmark (p₁=p₂=3, r₁=r₂=0.1, average cost), from the spectral solution with 32 Chebyshev points per side.
fig:stationary-precision: The early peak of h^(X,1) against precision: lag and depth of the minimum of the signal-noise channel as the observer’s own precision p₁ (solid) and the opponent’s p₂ (dashed) vary, the other held at 3.
fig:stationary-hankel: Singular values σₖ of the four one-sided pieces of h^(X,1), with an exactly rational kernel of degree two as control.
fig:stationary-refinement: The signal-noise piece of h^(X,1): grid solutions on successively finer grids (green) and the spectral solution with 24 points per side (black); spectral solutions with 8, 12, and 16 points (dashed) are indistinguishable from it at this scale.
fig:stationary-pinn: A neural-network solution compared with the Wiener–Hopf solution of the same system, with equation residuals below 2×10⁻³ at the fitting points.
fig:info-profit-loop: Information feedback around public order flow.
fig:price-flow: Order-flow news first becomes a normalized order-flow innovation, then a market-maker noise-state movement, and then a price movement.
fig:kb-kernels: Equilibria of the stationary system at trading cost 10⁻³.
fig:kb-impact-decomp: Price response to a unit order by one trader at age zero, decomposed by re-running the forward response with the opponents’ policies switched off (ε=0.1, ρ=0.1; the large cost smooths the kernels, and the decomposition is about shape).
fig:kb-wedge-decomp: The three terms of Theorem 4.10 for each trader’s order in stock one, by coordinate age and shock channel, in the generalist–specialist market at ρ=0.1: specialist solid, generalist dotted.
fig:kb-rho-ladder: The window artifact for one undiscounted trader: the unrevealed fundamental by shock age computed at ρ=0 on windows L=8, 16, and 32 falls linearly to zero exactly at L, so each window gives a different solution.
fig:ch5-logdev: One price in levels (left axis) and as a log deviation from its steady state x̄ (right axis), the unit used for every variable in this section.
fig:ch5-levels: Mean order under the three information structures, against the order-book noise s₃ (left, log scale) and against the volatility of nominal spending σᵤ (right, log scale).
fig:ch5-transmission: Response of the quote index to a unit shock in nominal spending at three volatilities of spending.
fig:ch5-idiosyncratic: Response of firm 0’s order to a unit shock in its own productivity at three volatilities of nominal spending.
fig:ch5-kernels: Four policy kernels of the strategic solution, by the age of the observation, at two resolutions of the age grid: the supplier’s quote weight on its order book, the buyer’s order weight on the transaction price, and the quote and order weights on the firm’s own productivity.
fig:mm-stationary: The stationary transparent and opaque markets against the inventory weight γ (ρ=0.5, ε=0.2, unit signal gain and noise, L=8, 60 cells).
fig:loop: The feedback loop of dispersed information.
